clinicalPearls: An acute, and sometimes chronic, kidney injury caused by deposition of calcium phosphate in the renal tubules after a large phosphate load
Classically follows oral sodium phosphate solutions used as bowel preparation for colonoscopy

Risk factors include older age, female sex, pre-existing chronic kidney disease, volume depletion, hypertension and drugs that affect renal haemodynamics such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and NSAIDs
Often presents as an unexplained subacute rise in creatinine weeks after the procedure, frequently without prominent symptoms
Transient hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia may be seen around the time of exposure
Renal biopsy, if performed, shows tubular and interstitial calcium phosphate deposition with tubular injury
Prevention is paramount: avoid oral sodium phosphate purgatives in at-risk patients and maintain good hydration
Management is supportive, namely stopping the offending preparation, correcting volume depletion and avoiding any further phosphate load
reference.pathophysiology: A large oral sodium phosphate load produces a transient surge in serum phosphate and delivers a high phosphate concentration to the renal tubules. When this coincides with volume depletion, which concentrates the tubular fluid and slows flow, and an alkaline distal tubular environment, calcium phosphate becomes supersaturated and precipitates within the tubular lumen and interstitium. The resulting intratubular obstruction and injury cause acute kidney injury, and persistent calcium phosphate deposition (nephrocalcinosis) can leave a lasting reduction in renal function. Patients with reduced baseline function or taking drugs that impair renal autoregulation are the most susceptible.
additionalDifferentials: Prerenal acute kidney injury from purgative-induced volume depletion
Acute tubular necrosis from other causes
Other crystalline nephropathies such as oxalate or urate deposition
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatinine trend before and after the bowel preparation
Serum calcium and phosphate around the time of exposure
Renal biopsy in unexplained cases, showing calcium phosphate deposition
Review of medications that impair renal perfusion
redFlags: Progressive or non-recovering acute kidney injury after bowel preparation
Severe electrolyte disturbance with marked hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia
Emergence of established chronic kidney disease after the episode
Oliguria or features of significant volume depletion
reference.prognosis: Some patients recover partially, but many are left with permanent chronic kidney disease, so prevention by avoiding oral sodium phosphate in at-risk individuals is far more effective than any treatment.
pitfalls: Using oral sodium phosphate purgatives in elderly patients, those with CKD, or those on ACE inhibitors, ARBs or diuretics
Failing to connect a delayed creatinine rise to an earlier bowel preparation
Allowing volume depletion during the preparation
Repeating a phosphate-based preparation in a previously affected patient
management: Discontinue and avoid oral sodium phosphate bowel preparations, using polyethylene glycol-based alternatives instead
Intravenous volume repletion to correct dehydration and enhance phosphate clearance
Withhold drugs that impair renal haemodynamics including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-receptor blockers, diuretics, and NSAIDs
Monitor serial creatinine and long-term renal function for persistent chronic kidney disease
Nephrology referral, with renal replacement therapy for severe acute kidney injury
Prevent recurrence by avoiding sodium phosphate preparations in older patients and those with chronic kidney disease or on interacting drugs
